name: Wei Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wei, 43, and I operate a wheeled loader at the large mine. I have a vocational certificate and have been on machines long enough to know when the stockpile has shifted, though I'm an ordinary operator, not a supervisor. I earn toward the lower end for this job. My partner works part-time at a bakery; our two children are in school, the mortgage takes a big bite, and we have less than a month saved. I use an AI tool now and then to explain a manual page, but I check it against the machine book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my workmates a few saved minutes won't change the loading line. We still need to fix wage rates that leave experienced operators short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My household budget already runs close to the edge. The bakery gives my partner hours, but a quiet week leaves our mortgage on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the loader and check the stockpile face each morning. I'd put my next overtime payment into our small emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the bills even if AI does almost nothing. Last term the children's shoes and a boiler repair landed together, and the account was nearly empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Nadiya that the shift hasn't changed and we should put the overtime in the emergency account. She knows the boiler bill took most of what we had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a small AI tool help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes I ask it to explain a hydraulic warning in plain words. Then I check the manual and call the fitter if the warning stays on; I wouldn't diagnose the machine from a chat alone.

feel: **Anxious** about bills despite a stable loader line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch will feel this first, but loaders will feel the new timings. Operators deserve a say before software sets shift targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loader still needs my hands, yet planners could squeeze more trucks into each hour. If that changes breaks or overtime, our income could shrink quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask an experienced dispatcher to show me the new schedule screen at work. I'd bring a week's loading times to the union meeting if targets become unrealistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the household can't absorb even a small lost shift. I'm open to a useful schedule, but I want the people doing the loading to have evidence when it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which target would you challenge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plan sometimes assumes every truck arrives on the dot, even when a wet stockpile slows us down. I'd note the delays for a week so the union representative can point to the ground conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to check it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If another dispatcher showed it working on real shifts, yes. I already use an AI tool occasionally for manual questions, but I wouldn't call a schedule accurate just because it looks neat.

feel: **Anxious** about losing paid hours to unrealistic targets.
S1.quote: I wouldn't call a schedule accurate just because it looks neat.
fieldNote: He sees **planning automation** reaching the loading bay through targets even before robots operate the machine.
He is open to a **demonstrated tool** and would bring measured loading delays to collective bargaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine for 2028 office plans and a separate 2031 loader plan. The union should secure paid retraining before anyone loses a machine seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, the AI could do the planning while I still load rock. At 48 in 2031, I expect fewer operators and I could be one of the cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training coordinator now about a water plant operator course with paid hours. I'd apply to the regional water utility during the first robot year if loader posts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, and I keep thinking about how little money we have if my shift disappears. There are few local mines, so I can't rely on a quick transfer. I still have a path to investigate with the water utility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the water utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Its pumping station is on my route home, and the job adverts ask for equipment experience. I don't know whether my certificate is enough, so I'd ask before paying for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the bakery wage would not meet our mortgage on its own. I'd need paid training or another paid job while I learn.

S2.quote: There are few local mines, so I can't rely on a quick transfer.

He seeks a reachable **water utility** job, but course cost and the mortgage make paid training essential.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to post 2034 replacement dates by machine, not rumours. We can use the time for paid certificates that other employers recognise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AI could handle shift plans and inspection records while I still drive. At 51 in 2034, the children will be older, but our mortgage still needs an income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book a meeting with the training coordinator this winter about a water operations certificate. I'd cut our summer holiday fund for one year and build a full month's emergency reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about today's money, but I could make a five-year warning useful if I knew the replacement schedule. The children would miss a trip more than I would, so I'd talk it through with them rather than quietly cancel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are choosing a closer holiday so we can protect the house and pay for my training if needed. They may complain, but they understand that the boiler already emptied our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before I have another paid offer. The mine wage still pays our mortgage each month. Some operators earn more, but I need another paid offer before leaving.

S3.quote: The mine wage still pays our mortgage each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2039 robots leave years for retraining if workers know the real dates. The mine and union should publish local job routes before the fleet changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, the records and plans may be automated while my loader still runs. At 56 in 2039, I may still need paid work, even with grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the loader and save any extra shift money this year. I'd visit the water utility recruitment desk next spring to ask which certificate it accepts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because our bank balance is thin today, though the robot date is far away. A decade gives me time to test another path without gambling the mortgage on a course tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait until 2039 to change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd visit the utility next spring and ask what their actual entry requirements are. I may stay on the loader for years, but I want a named route before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your partner be involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadiya knows when her bakery shifts are likely to be short, and we'd plan saving around those months. I'd show her the utility pay scale before accepting any offer, because a move has to cover the mortgage.

The mine and union should publish **local job routes** before the fleet changes.

At 56 in **2039**, I may still need paid work, even with grown children.

S4.quote: I want a named route before the robots arrive.
fieldNote: His **present budget** remains fragile even though hands-on robots are projected for 2039.
He wants to confirm the utility's actual **certificate** and pay requirements before leaving a mine wage that supports the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the 2031 robots could cut my loader hours while the children still rely on us and we have almost nothing saved. Paid training, real replacement dates and a local job lead would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the new job would pay enough. A certificate sounds fine, but I would check the utility's wage before moving because the mortgage doesn't wait for a career change.

headlineQuote: A certificate sounds fine, but I would check the utility's wage before moving because the mortgage doesn't wait for a career change.
portrait: Wei is a **43-year-old** experienced loader operator with a vocational certificate and lower pay than many peers.
His partner's bakery shifts vary; two school-age children, a **mortgage** and less than a month saved constrain every choice.
He tries **AI occasionally**, verifies it against the machine book and wants colleagues to demonstrate new scheduling tools.
A fast robot arrival prompts **training enquiries** and utility applications; longer warning helps him build reserves while keeping income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 robots could reduce loader work before he builds a household reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, firm replacement dates and a local job paying enough for the mortgage would help him change course.
